summary.text: Coulomb's law describes the force between two electrically charged particles at rest, often called the electrostatic or Coulomb force.
The force acts along the line joining the charges, pushing them apart if their signs match and pulling them together if they differ.
It follows an inverse-square rule like Newton's gravity, but electric forces can push or pull and are much stronger than gravity.

facts.label: First published
facts.value: 1785, by French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb

facts.label: Coulomb's instrument
facts.value: A torsion balance: a charged ball on a twisting fiber

facts.label: Distance rule
facts.value: Force shrinks with the square of the distance

facts.label: Earlier hint
facts.value: Priestley conjectured an inverse-square law in 1767

items.prompt: Two charged balls repel each other. You move them twice as far apart. How does the push between them change?

options.label: It falls to a quarter of what it was
It falls to half of what it was
It stays the same, as charges are fixed
It doubles, since they have more room

items.explain: The force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, so doubling the distance cuts it to a quarter.

items.prompt: You hold two balls that both carry a positive charge close together. What does the force between them do?

options.label: It pulls them together, as with gravity
It pushes them apart along the line joining them
It pushes them sideways, at right angles to the line
It does nothing until one of them starts moving

items.explain: Same-sign charges repel, and the force lies along the straight line joining the two bodies.

items.prompt: Coulomb hung a charged ball from a thin fiber and brought a second charged ball near. How did he work out the force?

options.label: He weighed the balls before and after the test
He timed how fast the balls fell to the floor
He measured how far the fiber twisted
He counted the sparks jumping between the balls

items.explain: The twist angle, together with the known force needed to twist the fiber that far, gave the force between the balls.

items.prompt: A friend says electric forces and gravity are the same kind of rule, so electric forces must always pull. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Electric forces never act over a distance at all
Electric forces are far weaker, so they can be ignored
Electric forces only act on objects that are moving
Electric forces can also push, depending on the signs

items.explain: Both follow an inverse-square law, but gravity always attracts while electric forces repel or attract depending on the charges.

items.prompt: A small charged bead sits near three other fixed charges. How do you find the total force on the bead?

options.label: Add up the three separate forces as vectors
Use only the force from the nearest charge
Average the three forces as plain numbers
Use the force from the largest charge alone

items.explain: Superposition says the net force is the vector sum of the forces each charge would exert alone.

items.prompt: Charge A pushes on charge B with a certain force. What does B do to A?

options.label: Nothing, since only A is charged enough
It pushes on A with a weaker force
It pulls on A with an equal force
It pushes on A with an equal force the other way

items.explain: By Newton's third law the force on the second charge is the exact opposite of the force on the first.
